opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things people underestimate when they first get excited about RL for agents.

With supervised fine-tuning, the cost structure is pretty predictable. You have a dataset of demonstrations, you do forward and backward passes over it, and you're done. The expensive part is often getting good data in the first place, but once you have it, the training itself is relatively cheap and very parallelizable.

Reinforcement learning is a different beast. The big cost isn't the gradient update. It's the rollouts. For every training step, you have the model actually *act*: generate long trajectories, call tools, interact with an environment, maybe run code or browse or query a database, and then score the result. With agents those trajectories can be long and multi-turn, so you're paying for a lot of inference, often with sampling several attempts per prompt so you get a useful learning signal. Then there's the environment itself. Spinning up sandboxes, executing tool calls, waiting on latency. That's compute and wall-clock time that SFT never touches.

On top of that you have the verifier or reward model cost, and the sample inefficiency. A lot of rollouts give you little signal, especially if the task is too hard and everything fails, or too easy and everything succeeds. So curriculum and task selection end up mattering a lot for cost, not just for quality.

So how I think about it practically: SFT first, almost always. Get the model into the right distribution so it knows the format, the tools, and roughly what good behavior looks like. That makes RL dramatically cheaper because your rollouts start from a place where some fraction actually succeed. Then use RL for the things SFT can't easily give you: robustness, recovering from mistakes, optimizing for an outcome instead of imitating a trace.

And I'd say the other lever is being smart about which problems really need RL. If you can write a clean verifier and the task has headroom, RL can be well worth it. If you can just collect or synthesize better demonstrations, that's often the cheaper path. It's less "RL versus SFT" and more about spending your RL compute where it buys you something imitation can't.

r001.rationale: The response explains that RL repeatedly generates agent trajectories, often sampling several attempts, and that many rollouts may fail or provide little signal—communicating repeated trial and error as a source of higher cost.

r002.rationale: It suggests using SFT, curriculum, and task selection to reduce cost, but does not clearly identify optimizing rollout execution itself as a way to reduce RL’s compute burden.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because when people first hear "RL" they immediately assume it's going to be wildly more expensive than SFT, and the answer is more nuanced than that.

The honest framing is that the cost structure is just different. With supervised fine-tuning, almost all of your cost is upfront, in the data. You have to go collect or synthesize those trajectories, you have to label them, filter them, and for agents especially that's painful because you need full multi-step traces with tool calls that actually succeed. The training itself is cheap, you're just doing next-token prediction over a fixed dataset. But if your data is bad, or doesn't cover the distribution you care about, you've spent all that money and the model still won't generalize.

With RL, the training loop is where the compute goes. You're rolling out the policy, you're running the environment, you're scoring those rollouts, and then you're updating. For agents, the rollouts are the dominant cost, not the gradient steps. A single episode might involve twenty, fifty tool calls, the model generating thousands of tokens, waiting on a sandbox or a browser or a code execution environment. So you're paying for inference at scale plus all the infrastructure to host those environments. That's the part people underestimate. The GPU math for the policy update is almost a rounding error compared to the sampling.

But here's the thing: you're trading human-labeled data for verifiers. If you have a reliable reward signal, like did the test pass, did the task get completed, did the answer match, you've essentially replaced an expensive labeling pipeline with a cheap automated check. And the model gets to discover solutions you never would have written down as demonstrations. So per unit of capability gained, RL can actually be more compute-efficient on tasks where verification is easier than demonstration.

In practice, we almost never do pure one or the other. The pattern that works is a solid SFT stage to get the model into the right region, so it can at least follow the agent format and use the tools without flailing, and then RL on top. Starting RL from a cold model is where the compute really explodes, because your success rate is near zero and most rollouts give you no signal. Good SFT shrinks the number of rollouts you need, which is where the real savings are.

And then a lot of the engineering work is about making those rollouts cheaper. Asynchronous rollouts so your GPUs aren't sitting idle waiting on an environment, batching, reusing partial trajectories, being smart about which tasks you sample from so you're not wasting budget on things the model already does well or has no hope of doing. That kind of systems work ends up mattering as much as the algorithm.

r001.rationale: It contrasts SFT’s mostly upfront data costs with RL’s compute-heavy loop of repeatedly rolling out the policy, scoring results, and updating it. This conveys trial-and-error as the source of RL’s added compute burden.

r002.rationale: It explicitly recommends making rollouts cheaper through asynchronous execution, batching, reusing partial trajectories, and more selective task sampling.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate the cost of generating experience from the cost of updating the model. With supervised fine-tuning, you have a fixed dataset, and you’re training against those examples. With reinforcement learning, you also have to generate trajectories, evaluate them, and then use that feedback to update the policy.

For agents, that experience-generation step can be substantial. A trajectory might involve multiple model calls, tool calls, and waiting for an environment to respond. So the cost isn’t just GPU compute; it’s also the time and infrastructure needed to run those interactions.

But the useful comparison is the cost of reaching a particular level of capability. If you have good demonstrations, supervised fine-tuning can be a very efficient starting point. Reinforcement learning becomes useful when you can evaluate success more easily than you can demonstrate exactly how to achieve it. Then the question is whether the improvement from that additional experience justifies the cost.

r001.rationale: The response says RL requires generating and evaluating trajectories, but does not clearly attribute its higher compute cost to repeated trial-and-error learning.

r002.rationale: The response describes experience generation costs but does not identify optimizing rollout execution as a way to reduce them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the cost of the training update from the cost of generating the experience. In supervised fine-tuning, you have a fixed set of examples, and you’re learning from those. With reinforcement learning, you also have to run the agent, collect trajectories, evaluate the outcomes, and then use that feedback to update the model.

For an agent, those trajectories can involve multiple model calls, tool calls, and interactions with an environment. So the cost depends quite a bit on how long those interactions are and how many attempts you need to get a useful learning signal. Comparing just the cost per training step misses a lot of that.

The question I’d ask is: what does it cost to reach a particular level of task success? If you have good demonstrations, supervised fine-tuning can be a very efficient starting point. Reinforcement learning becomes useful when you can evaluate success, but it’s harder to demonstrate every decision the agent should make along the way. You’re paying for exploration, and the important thing is whether that exploration produces enough improvement to justify the cost.

r001.rationale: It says reinforcement learning requires running the agent, collecting and evaluating trajectories, and paying for exploration and repeated attempts to get a useful learning signal.

r002.rationale: It notes that interaction length affects cost, but does not identify optimizing rollout execution as a way to reduce that burden.
